claim: PRC1 is essential for the specification of segmentally restricted spinal motor neuron (MN) subtypes.
source: We found that PRC1 is essential for the specification of segmentally restricted spinal motor neuron (MN) subtypes, while PRC2 activity is dispensable to maintain MN positional identities during terminal differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Ring1 mutant mice showing loss of MN subtype identities, as described throughout the manuscript including immunohistochemistry and RNAseq analyses.

claim: PRC2 activity is dispensable to maintain MN positional identities during terminal differentiation.
source: We found that PRC1 is essential for the specification of segmentally restricted spinal motor neuron (MN) subtypes, while PRC2 activity is dispensable to maintain MN positional identities during terminal differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from EzhMNΔ and EedNEΔ mice showing normal Hox expression patterns despite loss of PRC2 function.

claim: Mutation of the core PRC1 component Ring1 in mice leads to increased chromatin accessibility.
source: Mutation of the core PRC1 component Ring1 in mice leads to increased chromatin accessibility and ectopic expression of a broad variety of fates determinants, including Hox transcription factors, while neuronal class-specific features are maintained.
evidence: This claim is supported by ATACseq data showing increased chromatin accessibility at multiple loci in Ring1 mutant mice.

claim: Mutation of Ring1 leads to ectopic expression of a broad variety of fate determinants, including Hox transcription factors.
source: Mutation of the core PRC1 component Ring1 in mice leads to increased chromatin accessibility and ectopic expression of a broad variety of fates determinants, including Hox transcription factors, while neuronal class-specific features are maintained.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq and in situ hybridization data showing upregulation of multiple transcription factors including Hox genes in Ring1 mutants.

claim: Neuronal class-specific features are maintained in Ring1 mutants.
source: Mutation of the core PRC1 component Ring1 in mice leads to increased chromatin accessibility and ectopic expression of a broad variety of fates determinants, including Hox transcription factors, while neuronal class-specific features are maintained.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and RNAseq data showing preserved expression of pan-MN markers like Mnx1, Isl1/2, and Lhx3 in Ring1 mutants.

claim: Loss of MN subtype identities in Ring1 mutants is due to the suppression of Hox-dependent specification programs by derepressed Hox13 paralogs (Hoxa13, Hoxb13, Hoxc13, Hoxd13).
source: Loss of MN subtype identities in Ring1 mutants is due to the suppression of Hox-dependent specification programs by derepressed Hox13 paralogs (Hoxa13, Hoxb13, Hoxc13, Hoxd13).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data showing derepression of Hox13 paralogs, ChIPseq data showing Hoxc13 binding at rostral Hox genes, and functional experiments showing Hox13 paralogs can repress rostral Hox genes.

claim: PRC1 can function in the absence of de novo PRC2-dependent histone methylation to maintain chromatin topology and postmitotic neuronal fate.
source: These results indicate that PRC1 can function in the absence of de novo PRC2-dependent histone methylation to maintain chromatin topology and postmitotic neuronal fate.
evidence: This claim is supported by the observation that PRC2 mutants show normal MN specification despite loss of H3K27me3, while PRC1 mutants show severe defects, indicating PRC1 can function independently of PRC2.

claim: In embryonic stem cells, cell fate determinants are repressed through PRC activities.
source: In embryonic stem cells, cell fate determinants are repressed through PRC activities, and PRC-associated histone marks are subsequently removed from loci as cells differentiate (Boyer et al., 2006; Farcas et al., 2012; Tavares et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on PRC function in embryonic stem cells.

claim: PRC repression is maintained through cell division and after differentiation.
source: PRC repression is maintained through cell division and after differentiation and is thought to contribute to stable cellular memories of early patterning events (Ciabrelli et al., 2017; Coleman and Struhl, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on PRC function during development.

claim: A core set of transcription factors, including Mnx1, Isl1/2, and Lhx3, determines class-specific features of MNs, including neurotransmitter identity.
source: A core set of transcription factors, including Mnx1, Isl1/2, and Lhx3, determines class-specific features of MNs, including neurotransmitter identity (Shirasaki and Pfaff, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on MN specification.

claim: The diversification of MNs into hundreds of muscle-specific subtypes is achieved through a conserved network of Hox transcription factors differentially expressed along the rostrocaudal axis.
source: The subsequent diversification of MNs into hundreds of muscle-specific subtypes is achieved through a conserved network of Hox transcription factors differentially expressed along the rostrocaudal axis (Philippidou and Dasen, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on Hox function in MN diversification.

claim: During neural tube patterning, opposing gradients of retinoic acid (RA) and fibroblast growth factors (FGFs) provide spinal progenitors with a positional identity.
source: During neural tube patterning, opposing gradients of retinoic acid (RA) and fibroblast growth factors (FGFs) provide spinal progenitors with a positional identity (Bel-Vialar et al., 2002; Dasen et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on morphogen gradients in neural tube patterning.

claim: RA and FGF morphogens act, in part, by temporally and spatially depleting Polycomb-associated histone marks from Hox clusters.
source: These morphogens act, in part, by temporally and spatially depleting Polycomb-associated histone marks from Hox clusters (Mazzoni et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on morphogen regulation of Polycomb marks.

claim: As progenitors exit the cell cycle, MNs continue to express Hox genes, where they regulate repertoires of subtype-specific genes.
source: As progenitors exit the cell cycle, MNs continue to express Hox genes, where they regulate repertoires of subtype-specific genes (Catela et al., 2016; Dasen et al., 2005; Mendelsohn et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on Hox gene function in postmitotic MNs.

claim: Polycomb repression is initiated by PRC2, which methylates histone H3 at lysine-27 (H3K27me3).
source: Polycomb repression is initiated by PRC2, which methylates histone H3 at lysine-27 (H3K27me3), permitting recruitment of PRC1 through subunits that recognize this mark, leading to chromatin compaction at genes targeted for repression (Margueron and Reinberg, 2011; Schuettengruber et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on PRC2 function and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: H3K27me3 permits recruitment of PRC1 through subunits that recognize this mark, leading to chromatin compaction at genes targeted for repression.
source: Polycomb repression is initiated by PRC2, which methylates histone H3 at lysine-27 (H3K27me3), permitting recruitment of PRC1 through subunits that recognize this mark, leading to chromatin compaction at genes targeted for repression (Margueron and Reinberg, 2011; Schuettengruber et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on PRC1 recruitment and function.

claim: In embryonic stem (ES) cells, Hox gene clusters are initially covered by H3K27me3.
source: In embryonic stem (ES) cells, Hox gene clusters are initially covered by H3K27me3 and loss of PRC2 function leads to reduced PRC1 binding and ectopic Hox expression (Boyer et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on Hox regulation in ES cells.

claim: Loss of PRC2 function in ES cells leads to reduced PRC1 binding and ectopic Hox expression.
source: In embryonic stem (ES) cells, Hox gene clusters are initially covered by H3K27me3 and loss of PRC2 function leads to reduced PRC1 binding and ectopic Hox expression (Boyer et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on PRC2 function in ES cells.

claim: During mouse development, H3K27me3 marks are progressively removed from Hox clusters, allowing for the temporal and spatial activation of more caudal Hox genes during axis extension.
source: During mouse development, H3K27me3 marks are progressively removed from Hox clusters, allowing for the temporal and spatial activation of more caudal Hox genes during axis extension (Soshnikova and Duboule, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on Hox regulation during development.

claim: The progressive removal of PRC2-associated histone marks is recapitulated in ES cell-derived MNs (ESC-MNs).
source: The progressive removal of PRC2-associated histone marks is also recapitulated in ES cell-derived MNs (ESC-MNs), where RA functions to deplete H3K27me3 from rostral Hox1-Hox5 paralogs, while FGF removes H3K27me3 from more caudal Hox genes through Cdx proteins (Mazzoni et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on Hox regulation in ESC-MNs.

claim: In ESC-MNs, RA functions to deplete H3K27me3 from rostral Hox1-Hox5 paralogs.
source: The progressive removal of PRC2-associated histone marks is also recapitulated in ES cell-derived MNs (ESC-MNs), where RA functions to deplete H3K27me3 from rostral Hox1-Hox5 paralogs, while FGF removes H3K27me3 from more caudal Hox genes through Cdx proteins (Mazzoni et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on morphogen regulation of Hox genes.

claim: FGF removes H3K27me3 from more caudal Hox genes through Cdx proteins in ESC-MNs.
source: The progressive removal of PRC2-associated histone marks is also recapitulated in ES cell-derived MNs (ESC-MNs), where RA functions to deplete H3K27me3 from rostral Hox1-Hox5 paralogs, while FGF removes H3K27me3 from more caudal Hox genes through Cdx proteins (Mazzoni et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on FGF regulation of Hox genes.

claim: Loss of PRC2 affects the viability of ESC-MNs.
source: Although loss of PRC2 affects the viability of ESC-MNs, a hypomorphic mutation in the PRC2 component Suz12 leads to ectopic Hox expression (Mazzoni et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on PRC2 function in ESC-MNs.

claim: A hypomorphic mutation in the PRC2 component Suz12 leads to ectopic Hox expression in ESC-MNs.
source: Although loss of PRC2 affects the viability of ESC-MNs, a hypomorphic mutation in the PRC2 component Suz12 leads to ectopic Hox expression (Mazzoni et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on Suz12 function.

claim: The core subunit of PRC1, Ring1, binds to one of six Polycomb group Ring finger (Pcgf) proteins.
source: The core subunit of PRC1, Ring1, binds to one of six Polycomb group Ring finger (Pcgf) proteins (Gao et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on PRC1 composition.

claim: PRC1 containing Pcgf4 interacts with Cbx proteins (canonical PRC1) which recognize H3K27me3.
source: PRC1 containing Pcgf4 interacts with Cbx proteins (canonical PRC1) which recognize H3K27me3 (Bernstein et al., 2006; Morey et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on canonical PRC1 composition and function.

claim: Variant forms of PRC1 containing Rybp can inhibit incorporation of Cbx proteins into PRC1, and bind target loci independent of H3K27me3.
source: Variant forms of PRC1 containing Rybp can inhibit incorporation of Cbx proteins into PRC1, and bind target loci independent of H3K27me3 (Tavares et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on variant PRC1 function.

claim: Pcgf4 (Bmi1) is required to establish rostral boundaries of Hox expression in differentiating MNs.
source: We previously found that a PRC1 component, Pcgf4 (Bmi1), is required to establish rostral boundaries of Hox expression in differentiating MNs (Golden and Dasen, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work from the authors' lab.

claim: Deletion of Ezh2 from MN progenitors had no apparent impact on fate specification.
source: By contrast, deletion of a core PRC2 component, Ezh2, from MN progenitors had no apparent impact on fate specification, possibly due to compensation by Ezh1 (Shen et al., 2008), or through use of variant PRC1 containing Rybp.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and speculation about potential mechanisms.

claim: H3K27me3 was selectively depleted from progenitors and post-mitotic MNs by E11.5 in EzhMNΔ mice.
source: We confirmed MN-restricted loss of PRC2 activity by examining the pattern of H3K27me3, which was selectively depleted from progenitors and post-mitotic MNs by E11.5 (Figure 1A and B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1B and quantification in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Expression of Mnx1 and Slc18a3 (Vacht) were grossly unchanged in EzhMNΔ mice.
source: Expression of Mnx1 and Slc18a3 (Vacht), two general markers of MN identity, were grossly unchanged in EzhMNΔ mice (Figure 1C, D and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1C, D and quantification in Figure 1G.

claim: The MN columnar subtype determinants Hoxc6, Hoxc9, and Hoxc10 were all expressed in their normal domains in EzhMNΔ mice.
source: We next analyzed expression of Hox proteins in EzhMNΔ mice and found that the MN columnar subtype determinants Hoxc6, Hoxc9, and Hoxc10, were all expressed in their normal domains (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1E, F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: In EedNEΔ mice, H3K27me3 was depleted from spinal progenitors and postmitotic neurons by E11.5.
source: In EedNEΔ mice, H3K27me3 was depleted from spinal progenitors and postmitotic neurons by E11.5, with some H3K27me3 present in the floor plate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: In EedNEΔ mice, the number of Mnx1+ cells, and pattern of Hoxc6, Hoxc9, and Hoxc10 in MNs were unaffected.
source: In EedNEΔ mice, the number of Mnx1+ cells, and pattern of Hoxc6, Hoxc9, and Hoxc10 in MNs were unaffected, similar to EzhMNΔ mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, H-J).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, H-J.

claim: In Ring1MNΔ mice, Rnf2 (Ring1B) protein was selectively removed from progenitors and post-mitotic MNs.
source: In Ring1MNΔ mice, Rnf2 (Ring1B) protein was selectively removed from progenitors and post-mitotic MNs (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The number of Mnx1+ MNs and pattern of Slc18a3 expression were similar to controls in Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: The number of Mnx1+ MNs and pattern of Slc18a3 expression were similar to controls in Ring1MNΔ mice (Figure 1J, K and N).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1J, K and quantification in Figure 1N.

claim: In Ring1MNΔ mice, Hox proteins normally expressed by forelimb-innervating brachial MNs were not detected.
source: By contrast, Hox proteins normally expressed by forelimb-innervating brachial MNs were not detected, while thoracic and lumbar Hox proteins were ectopically expressed in more rostral MNs (Figure 1L, M and O–T, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C-E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1L, M, O-T and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C-E.

claim: Thoracic and lumbar Hox proteins were ectopically expressed in more rostral MNs in Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: By contrast, Hox proteins normally expressed by forelimb-innervating brachial MNs were not detected, while thoracic and lumbar Hox proteins were ectopically expressed in more rostral MNs (Figure 1L, M and O–T, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C-E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1L, M, O-T and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C-E.

claim: Brachial-level Hox proteins (Hoxc4, Hoxa5, Hoxc6 and Hoxc8) were selectively depleted from MNs in Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: Brachial-level Hox proteins (Hoxc4, Hoxa5, Hoxc6 and Hoxc8), were selectively depleted from MNs, while thoracic and lumbar Hox determinants, (Hoxc9, Hoxc10, and Hoxd10) were derepressed in brachial segments (Figure 1Q–T).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1Q-T.

claim: Thoracic and lumbar Hox determinants (Hoxc9, Hoxc10, and Hoxd10) were derepressed in brachial segments in Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: Brachial-level Hox proteins (Hoxc4, Hoxa5, Hoxc6 and Hoxc8), were selectively depleted from MNs, while thoracic and lumbar Hox determinants, (Hoxc9, Hoxc10, and Hoxd10) were derepressed in brachial segments (Figure 1Q–T).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1Q-T.

claim: Brachial MNs co-expressed Hoxc9 and Hoxc10 in Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: Brachial MNs also co-expressed Hoxc9 and Hoxc10, which are normally restricted to thoracic and lumbar segments, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: At thoracic levels, Hoxc9 expression was attenuated and Hoxd10 was ectopically expressed in Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: At thoracic levels, Hoxc9 expression was attenuated and Hoxd10 was ectopically expressed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Loss of Ring1 causes a derepression of caudal Hox genes, leading to co-expression of caudal Hox proteins in brachial MNs, without affecting pan-MN molecular features.
source: These results show that loss of Ring1 causes a derepression of caudal Hox genes, leading to co-expression of caudal Hox proteins in brachial MNs, without affecting pan-MN molecular features (Figure 1O).
evidence: This claim is supported by the collective immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 1 and summarized in Figure 1O.

claim: Expression of Rybp under Mnx1 led to ectopic Hoxc9 and Hoxc10 expression at brachial levels in chick.
source: Expression of Rybp under Mnx1 led to ectopic Hoxc9 and Hoxc10 expression at brachial levels (Figure 1V).
evidence: This claim is supported by chick electroporation experiments shown in Figure 1V.

claim: Co-electroporation of Mnx1-Rybp and Mnx1-Cbx2 at equivalent plasmid concentration resulted in no ectopic Hoxc9 in brachial segments.
source: To test this, we co-electroporated Mnx1-Rybp and Mnx1-Cbx2 at equivalent plasmid concentration, and no longer observed ectopic Hoxc9 in brachial segments (Figure 1X).
evidence: This claim is supported by chick electroporation experiments shown in Figure 1X.

claim: Combined deletion of Rybp and Yaf2 did not affect MN generation, Hoxc6, Hoxc9, or Hoxc10 expression.
source: Combined deletion of Rybp and Yaf2 did not affect MN generation, Hoxc6, Hoxc9, or Hoxc10 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data from Rybp/Yaf2MNΔ mice shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Canonical PRC1 maintains appropriate Hox expression in MNs.
source: These findings indicate that canonical PRC1 maintains appropriate Hox expression, while variant PRC1 and PRC2 do not contribute to rostrocaudal patterning at the time of MN differentiation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective data showing Ring1 mutant phenotypes, Rybp overexpression effects, and lack of phenotypes in Rybp/Yaf2 and PRC2 mutants.

claim: Variant PRC1 and PRC2 do not contribute to rostrocaudal patterning at the time of MN differentiation.
source: These findings indicate that canonical PRC1 maintains appropriate Hox expression, while variant PRC1 and PRC2 do not contribute to rostrocaudal patterning at the time of MN differentiation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of phenotypes in Rybp/Yaf2MNΔ and PRC2 mutant mice.

claim: In Ring1MNΔ mice, Foxp1 expression is lost from brachial and thoracic MNs, and markedly reduced in lumbar MNs.
source: In Ring1MNΔ mice, Foxp1 expression is lost from brachial and thoracic MNs, and markedly reduced in lumbar MNs (Figure 2A, B and G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2A, B, G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In EzhMNΔ, EedNEΔ, and Rybp/Yaf2MNΔ mice, Foxp1 expression was maintained.
source: By contrast, in EzhMNΔ, EedNEΔ, and Rybp/Yaf2MNΔ mice, Foxp1 expression was maintained, consistent with the preservation of normal Hox profiles in these mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: In Ring1MNΔ mice, expression of the LMC marker Raldh2 was lost at brachial levels.
source: In Ring1MNΔ mice, expression of the LMC marker Raldh2 was lost at brachial levels, and the thoracic PGC marker nNos was not detected (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The thoracic PGC marker nNos was not detected in Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: In Ring1MNΔ mice, expression of the LMC marker Raldh2 was lost at brachial levels, and the thoracic PGC marker nNos was not detected (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Expression of determinants of respiratory phrenic MNs (Scip+ Isl1/2+) was markedly depleted in Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: Moreover, expression of determinants of respiratory phrenic MNs (Scip+ Isl1/2+), was markedly depleted, and likely contributes to the perinatal lethality of Ring1MNΔ mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Ring1 deletion leads to a loss of genes acting downstream of Hox function in MNs.
source: These results indicate that Ring1 deletion leads to a loss of genes acting downstream of Hox function in MNs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the loss of Hox-dependent markers like Foxp1, Raldh2, and nNos in Ring1 mutants.

claim: In Ring1MNΔ mice, MMC neurons (Lhx3+ Mnx1+) were generated at normal numbers in thoracic segments.
source: In Ring1MNΔ mice, MMC neurons (Lhx3+ Mnx1+) were generated at normal numbers in thoracic segments, while the number of HMC neurons (Isl1/2+ Mnx1+ Lhx3-) was increased in thoracic and brachial segments (Figure 2E, F and H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data and quantification shown in Figure 2E, F, H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The number of HMC neurons (Isl1/2+ Mnx1+ Lhx3-) was increased in thoracic and brachial segments in Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: In Ring1MNΔ mice, MMC neurons (Lhx3+ Mnx1+) were generated at normal numbers in thoracic segments, while the number of HMC neurons (Isl1/2+ Mnx1+ Lhx3-) was increased in thoracic and brachial segments (Figure 2E, F and H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data and quantification shown in Figure 2E, F, H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The increase in HMC neurons in Ring1 mutants is likely due to a reversion of presumptive Hox-dependent subtypes to an HMC fate.
source: The increase in HMC neurons in Ring1 mutants is likely due to a reversion of presumptive Hox-dependent subtypes to an HMC fate, similar to mice in which Hox function is disrupted (Dasen et al., 2008; Hanley et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison to previous studies on Hox mutants and represents a logical interpretation of the data.

claim: A small population of medial neurons coexpressed Isl1/2, Mnx1, and Lhx3 in Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: We also observed a small population of medial neurons that coexpressed Isl1/2, Mnx1, and Lhx3 (Figure 2E, F and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2E, F and quantification in Figure 2H.

claim: Mutation in Ring1 depletes Hox-dependent subtypes, with the remaining MNs having a more ancestral axial or ambiguous subtype identity.
source: Mutation in Ring1 therefore depletes Hox-dependent subtypes, with the remaining MNs having a more ancestral axial or ambiguous subtype identity (Figure 2P).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective data on MN subtype markers and summarized in Figure 2P.

claim: In Ring1MNΔ mice, only three nerve branches (radial, median, and ulnar) were visible but appeared prematurely truncated and unbranched.
source: In Ring1MNΔ mice, only three nerve branches, radial, median, and ulnar were visible but appeared prematurely truncated and unbranched (Figure 2K).
evidence: This claim is supported by wholemount imaging of Mnx1-GFP labeled axons shown in Figure 2K.

claim: In the trunk, innervation of sympathetic chain ganglia was lost in Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: In the trunk, innervation of sympathetic chain ganglia was lost, consistent with a loss of PGC fates (Figure 2L and M).
evidence: This claim is supported by wholemount imaging shown in Figure 2L and M.

claim: Projections to dorsal and ventral axial muscles by MMC and HMC subtypes were maintained in Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: Projections to dorsal and ventral axial muscles by MMC and HMC subtypes were maintained in Ring1MNΔ mice, and HMC axons were thicker and shorter than in controls (Figure 2N and O, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by wholemount imaging shown in Figure 2N, O and quantification in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: HMC axons were thicker and shorter than in controls in Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: Projections to dorsal and ventral axial muscles by MMC and HMC subtypes were maintained in Ring1MNΔ mice, and HMC axons were thicker and shorter than in controls (Figure 2N and O, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by wholemount imaging shown in Figure 2N, O and quantification in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Loss of Ring1 causes severe defects in innervation pattern, while the trajectories of axial MNs are relatively spared.
source: Loss of Ring1 therefore causes severe defects in innervation pattern, while the trajectories of axial MNs are relatively spared.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective data on motor axon projections in Ring1 mutants.

claim: A total of 1001 genes were upregulated and 641 genes were downregulated in Ring1MNΔ mice (log2-FC > 2, FDR < 0.1).
source: We identified a total of 1001 upregulated and 641 downregulated genes in Ring1MNΔ mice (log2-FC > 2, FDR < 0.1), with 391 genes upregulated in all three segmental regions, compared to 46 genes that were commonly downregulated (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 3A-C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: 391 genes were upregulated in all three segmental regions in Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: We identified a total of 1001 upregulated and 641 downregulated genes in Ring1MNΔ mice (log2-FC > 2, FDR < 0.1), with 391 genes upregulated in all three segmental regions, compared to 46 genes that were commonly downregulated (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 46 genes were commonly downregulated in all three segmental regions in Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: We identified a total of 1001 upregulated and 641 downregulated genes in Ring1MNΔ mice (log2-FC > 2, FDR < 0.1), with 391 genes upregulated in all three segmental regions, compared to 46 genes that were commonly downregulated (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Many upregulated genes are shared between each segment, while downregulated genes tended to be segment-specific.
source: Thus, many upregulated genes are shared between each segment, while downregulated genes tended to be segment-specific.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the RNAseq data showing overlap between segments.

claim: 76% of the top 100 derepressed genes (by log2-FC) at brachial levels encode transcription factors.
source: Strikingly, 76% of the top 100 derepressed genes (by log2-FC) at brachial levels encode transcription factors, and include genes normally involved in the specification of spinal interneurons (e.g. Gata3, Shox2, Lhx2), brain regions (Foxg1, Six6, Lhx8), and non-neuronal lineages (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of RNAseq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Core molecular determinants of MN class identity are preserved in Ring1 mutants.
source: Although a variety of cell fate determinants were derepressed in Ring1MNΔ mice, our RNAseq analyses provide further evidence that core molecular determinants of MN class identity are preserved in Ring1 mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data showing no significant changes in key MN transcription factors.

claim: There were no significant changes in transcription factors (Isl1, Isl2, Mnx1, Lhx3, Lhx4), guidance molecules (Slit2, Robo1, Robo2, Dcc) and neurotransmitter genes (Chat, Acly) associated with pan-MN features in Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: We found no significant changes in transcription factors (Isl1, Isl2, Mnx1, Lhx3, Lhx4), guidance molecules (Slit2, Robo1, Robo2, Dcc) and neurotransmitter genes (Chat, Acly) associated with pan-MN features (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There was a modest decrease in expression of Slc18a3 in Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: There was a modest decrease in expression of Slc18a3 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Expression of genes that mark other excitatory (Slc17a7, Slc17a6) or inhibitory (Slc32a1, Gad2, Gad1) neuronal classes were not markedly derepressed in Ring1 mutants.
source: Expression of genes that mark other excitatory (Slc17a7, Slc17a6) or inhibitory (Slc32a1, Gad2, Gad1,) neuronal classes were not markedly derepressed in Ring1 mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Expression of genes associated with MN subtype identities was decreased in Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: By contrast, expression of genes associated with MN subtype identities was decreased in Ring1MNΔ mice, including genes that mark limb-innervating (e.g. Foxp1, Etv4, Raldh2, Runx1), thoracic-specific (Nos1, Cyp26b), and respiratory (Alcam, Ptn) subtypes (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Gata3, Lhx8, and Lhx2 were markedly upregulated in MNs of Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: We found that Gata3, Lhx8, and Lhx2 were markedly upregulated in MNs of Ring1MNΔ mice (Figure 4A–F), while other genes (Foxg1, Six6, Pitx2, Shox2, Nkx2.1) showed less prominent, but detectable, ectopic expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-J).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4A-F.

claim: Foxg1, Six6, Pitx2, Shox2, and Nkx2.1 showed less prominent, but detectable, ectopic expression in Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: We found that Gata3, Lhx8, and Lhx2 were markedly upregulated in MNs of Ring1MNΔ mice (Figure 4A–F), while other genes (Foxg1, Six6, Pitx2, Shox2, Nkx2.1) showed less prominent, but detectable, ectopic expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-J).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-J.

claim: Rgs4, Uts2b, Vat1, and Gabra2 were expressed by MNs of control embryos, and were downregulated in Ring1 mutants.
source: We found Rgs4, Uts2b, Vat1, and Gabra2 were expressed by MNs of control embryos, and were downregulated in Ring1 mutants (Figure 4G–L, Figure 4—figure supplement 1K,L).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4G-L and Figure 4—figure supplement 1K, L.

claim: Core features of MN identity are preserved in Ring1MNΔ mice, but subtype diversification programs are selectively disrupted.
source: These results indicate that despite the derepression of multiple fate determinants in Ring1MNΔ mice, core features of MN identity are preserved, but that subtype diversification programs are selectively disrupted.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective RNAseq and in situ hybridization data.

claim: Rostral Hox genes (Hox4-Hox8 paralogs) were reduced in brachial MNs of Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: Consistent with the analysis of Hox protein expression, rostral Hox genes (Hox4-Hox8 paralogs) were reduced in brachial MNs of Ring1MNΔ mice, while caudal Hox genes (Hox10-Hox13 paralogs) were derepressed (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Caudal Hox genes (Hox10-Hox13 paralogs) were derepressed in brachial MNs of Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: Consistent with the analysis of Hox protein expression, rostral Hox genes (Hox4-Hox8 paralogs) were reduced in brachial MNs of Ring1MNΔ mice, while caudal Hox genes (Hox10-Hox13 paralogs) were derepressed (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Derepression of caudal Hox genes from each of the four vertebrate Hox clusters was observed in Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: We observed derepression of caudal Hox genes from each of the four vertebrate Hox clusters, including genes not normally detectable in the ventral spinal cord (e.g. HoxB genes) (Dasen et al., 2005; Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: The extent of caudal Hox derepression correlated with the relative position of genes within a cluster, with Hox13 paralogs displaying the most pronounced derepression.
source: The extent of caudal Hox derepression correlated with the relative position of genes within a cluster, with Hox13 paralogs (Hoxa13, Hoxb13, Hoxc13, Hoxd13) displaying the most pronounced derepression in Ring1MNΔ mice (by FC), relative to other caudal Hox genes (Figure 5B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The marked derepression of Hox13 paralogs was observed in each of the three segmental levels analyzed.
source: The marked derepression of Hox13 paralogs was observed in each of the three segmental levels we analyzed, while Hox10 paralogs (Hoxa10, Hoxc10, and Hoxd10) were selectively derepressed in brachial and thoracic segments (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Hox10 paralogs (Hoxa10, Hoxc10, and Hoxd10) were selectively derepressed in brachial and thoracic segments in Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: The marked derepression of Hox13 paralogs was observed in each of the three segmental levels we analyzed, while Hox10 paralogs (Hoxa10, Hoxc10, and Hoxd10) were selectively derepressed in brachial and thoracic segments (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: In controls, Hoxc13 is restricted to sacral segments.
source: In controls Hoxc13 is restricted to sacral segments, while Hoxb13 is not detected in MNs (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Hoxb13 is not detected in MNs in controls.
source: In controls Hoxc13 is restricted to sacral segments, while Hoxb13 is not detected in MNs (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In Ring1MNΔ mice, both Hoxb13 and Hoxc13 were de-repressed in MNs throughout the rostrocaudal axis.
source: In Ring1MNΔ mice, both Hoxb13 and Hoxc13, were de-repressed in MNs throughout the rostrocaudal axis (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Ectopic expression of Hoxb13 and Hoxc13 was not observed in EzhMNΔ mice.
source: By contrast, ectopic expression of Hoxb13 and Hoxc13 was not observed in EzhMNΔ mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: Ectopic expression of Hox13 paralogs in Ring1 mutants is associated with a loss of rostral Hox gene expression.
source: Thus, ectopic expression of Hox13 paralogs in Ring1 mutants is associated with a loss of rostral Hox gene expression.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective data showing derepression of Hox13 paralogs and loss of rostral Hox expression.

claim: In control samples, there was a progressive opening of caudal Hox genes in more rostral segments.
source: In control samples, we observed a progressive opening of caudal Hox genes in more rostral segments. For example, the accessibility of Hoxc9 and Hoxa9 increases from brachial to thoracic segments, while Hoxc10, Hoxc11, and Hoxa10 are more accessible in lumbar segments (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATACseq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: A total of 2305 loci gained accessibility in Ring1MNΔ embryos.
source: We identified a total of 2305 loci that gained accessibility in Ring1MNΔ embryos, 324 (14%) of which were common to all three segmental levels (Figure 6A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATACseq analysis shown in Figure 6A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: 324 (14%) loci that gained accessibility were common to all three segmental levels in Ring1MNΔ embryos.
source: We identified a total of 2305 loci that gained accessibility in Ring1MNΔ embryos, 324 (14%) of which were common to all three segmental levels (Figure 6A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATACseq analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Common genes that gained accessibility included caudal Hox genes (Hoxa13, Hoxc13) and other transcription factors (e.g. Foxg1, Lhx2, Pitx2) that were derepressed in RNAseq analyses.
source: Common genes included caudal Hox genes (Hoxa13, Hoxc13) and other transcription factors (e.g. Foxg1, Lhx2, Pitx2) that were derepressed in our RNAseq analyses (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATACseq data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: 1264 loci lost accessibility in Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: We also identified 1264 loci that lost accessibility in Ring1MNΔ mice, 39 (3%) of which were common to all three segments (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATACseq analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: 39 (3%) loci that lost accessibility were common to all three segments in Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: We also identified 1264 loci that lost accessibility in Ring1MNΔ mice, 39 (3%) of which were common to all three segments (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATACseq analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Loss of Ring1 leads to increased accessibility in many genes that are shared among each segment, while genes that lose accessibility tend to be segment-specific.
source: Thus, similar to our RNAseq results, loss of Ring1 leads to increased accessibility in many genes that are shared among each segment, while genes that lose accessibility tend to be segment-specific.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the ATACseq data showing overlap between segments.

claim: 18% (148/813) of genes that were ectopically expressed at brachial segments also gained accessibility in Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: We found that 18% (148/813) of genes that were ectopically expressed at brachial segments also gained accessibility in Ring1MNΔ mice (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of RNAseq and ATACseq data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: 19 genes, including Hoxa13 and Hoxc13, were derepressed and gained accessibility in all three segments.
source: We found 19 genes, including Hoxa13 and Hoxc13, were derepressed and gained accessibly in all three segments (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of RNAseq and ATACseq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 73 genes were upregulated and gained accessibility in brachial and thoracic MNs, 56 (77%) of which encode transcription factors.
source: We identified 73 genes, 56 (77%) of which encode transcription factors, including each of the caudal Hox genes we found by RNAseq (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of RNAseq and ATACseq data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The gain of accessibility at transcription factor-encoding genes was prominent near transcription start sites.
source: The gain of accessibility at transcription factor-encoding genes was prominent near transcription start sites (Figure 6C), and regions that gained accessibility in Ring1MNΔ neurons correspond to regions shown to be bound by Rnf2 (Ring1B) in ES cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D; Bonev et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATACseq data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Regions that gained accessibility in Ring1MNΔ neurons correspond to regions shown to be bound by Rnf2 (Ring1B) in ES cells.
source: The gain of accessibility at transcription factor-encoding genes was prominent near transcription start sites (Figure 6C), and regions that gained accessibility in Ring1MNΔ neurons correspond to regions shown to be bound by Rnf2 (Ring1B) in ES cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D; Bonev et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of ATACseq data with published ChIPseq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Hox13 paralogs showed pronounced increases in accessibility, with each of the four Hox13 paralogs gaining accessibility in each of the three segmental levels.
source: In agreement with our RNAseq analysis, Hox13 paralogs showed pronounced increases in accessibility, with each of the four Hox13 paralogs gaining accessibility in each of the three segmental levels (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATACseq data shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: Rostral Hox4-Hox8 paralogs, which are transcriptionally downregulated in Ring1 mutants, were not among the targets that lost accessibility.
source: By contrast, rostral Hox4-Hox8 paralogs, which are transcriptionally downregulated in Ring1 mutants, were not among that targets that lost accessibility (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATACseq data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Reduced expression of rostral Hox4-Hox8 paralogs in Ring1 mutants is not due to a loss in chromatin accessibility.
source: These results suggest that reduced expression of rostral Hox4-Hox8 paralogs in Ring1 mutants is not due to a loss in chromatin accessibility.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the ATACseq data showing no loss of accessibility at rostral Hox genes.

claim: Hoxa4, Hoxa5, Hoxc4, and Hoxc5 expression were markedly reduced after Dox-induced Hoxc13 expression in MN progenitors.
source: RNAseq analyses revealed that Hoxa4, Hoxa5, Hoxc4, and Hoxc5 expression were markedly reduced after Dox-induced Hoxc13 expression in MN progenitors, compared to non-induced ESC-MNs (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data from ESC-MNs shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: ChIPseq analysis indicates that Hoxc13 can bind at multiple Hox genes.
source: This repressive effect also appears to be direct, as ChIPseq analysis indicates that Hoxc13 can bind at multiple Hox genes (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIPseq data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: At Hoxc4, Hoxc5, Hoxa4, and Hoxa5, Hoxc13 bound sites correspond to regions that are accessible in both control and Ring1 mutant MNs.
source: At Hoxc4, Hoxc5, Hoxa4, and Hoxa5, Hoxc13 bound sites correspond to regions that are accessible in both control and Ring1 mutant MNs (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of ChIPseq and ATACseq data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Hox13 proteins repress rostral Hox genes, in part, through binding at pre-existing accessible regions.
source: Hox13 proteins therefore appear to repress rostral Hox genes, in part, through binding at pre-existing accessible regions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the ChIPseq and ATACseq data showing Hoxc13 binding at accessible regions.

claim: Hoxa13 and Hoxb13 cell-autonomously repressed expression of brachial, thoracic, and lumbar Hox proteins (Hoxc4, Hoxa5, Hoxc6, Hoxc8, Hoxc9, and Hoxc10) in chick.
source: We electroporated pCAGGs-Hoxa13-ires-nucGFP or pCAGGs-Hoxb13-ires-nucGFP and found that both cell-autonomously repressed expression of brachial, thoracic, and lumbar Hox proteins (Hoxc4, Hoxa5, Hoxc6, Hoxc8, Hoxc9, and Hoxc10) (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by chick electroporation experiments shown in Figure 7B-D.

claim: Misexpression of Hoxa13 and Hoxb13 did not affect expression of the general MN markers Isl1/2 and Mnx1 in chick.
source: By contrast, misexpression of Hoxa13 and Hoxb13 did not affect expression of the general MN markers Isl1/2 and Mnx1 (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by chick electroporation experiments shown in Figure 7B-D.

claim: Hox13 paralogs can repress multiple Hox genes, and likely contribute to the MN fate specification defects of Ring1MNΔ mice.
source: These results indicate that Hox13 paralogs can repress multiple Hox genes, and likely contribute to the MN fate specification defects of Ring1MNΔ mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective data on Hox13 function in ESC-MNs and chick experiments.

claim: Genetic depletion of PRC2 components has no discernible impact on neural class or subtype diversification programs at the time of MN differentiation.
source: In this study, we found that genetic depletion of PRC2 components has no discernable impact on neural class or subtype diversification programs at the time of MN differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the collective data from EzhMNΔ and EedNEΔ mice showing normal MN specification.

claim: Ring1 is required to restrict transcription factor expression in the CNS.
source: By contrast, a core PRC1 subunit, Ring1, is required to restrict transcription factor expression in the CNS, maintain neuronal subtype-specific chromatin topology, and determine rostrocaudal boundaries of Hox expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data showing derepression of multiple transcription factors in Ring1 mutants.

claim: Ring1 is required to maintain neuronal subtype-specific chromatin topology.
source: By contrast, a core PRC1 subunit, Ring1, is required to restrict transcription factor expression in the CNS, maintain neuronal subtype-specific chromatin topology, and determine rostrocaudal boundaries of Hox expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by ATACseq data showing increased chromatin accessibility in Ring1 mutants.

claim: Ring1 is required to determine rostrocaudal boundaries of Hox expression.
source: By contrast, a core PRC1 subunit, Ring1, is required to restrict transcription factor expression in the CNS, maintain neuronal subtype-specific chromatin topology, and determine rostrocaudal boundaries of Hox expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and RNAseq data showing altered Hox expression in Ring1 mutants.

claim: Deletion of Ring1 leads to increased chromatin accessibility and derepression of a broad variety of cell fate determinants, while class-specific features of MNs are preserved.
source: Deletion of Ring1 leads to increased chromatin accessibility and derepression of a broad variety of cell fate determinants, while class-specific features of MNs are preserved.
evidence: This claim is supported by ATACseq and RNAseq data from Ring1 mutants.

claim: The derepression of caudal Hox genes in Ring1 mutants leads to the suppression of MN subtype diversification programs.
source: The derepression of caudal Hox genes in Ring1 mutants leads to the suppression of MN subtype diversification programs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the collective data showing derepression of caudal Hox genes and loss of subtype-specific markers.

claim: PRC1 function is essential during terminal differentiation to specify the transcriptional identities of motor neurons.
source: These findings indicate that PRC1 function is essential during terminal differentiation to specify the transcriptional identities of motor neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective data showing severe specification defects in Ring1 mutants.

claim: Once a class identity has been established, ectopic expression of fate determinants is insufficient to respecify basic neuronal features, such as neurotransmitter identity.
source: This observation suggests that once a class identity has been established, ectopic expression of fate determinants is insufficient to respecify basic neuronal features, such as neurotransmitter identity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that MN class markers are preserved despite derepression of multiple fate determinants in Ring1 mutants.

claim: In C. elegans, the ability of transcription factors to reprogram neuronal class identity requires removal of histone deacetylase proteins.
source: In C. elegans the ability of transcription factors to reprogram neuronal class identity requires removal of histone deacetylase proteins (Tursun et al., 2011), suggesting that additional regulatory constraints, such as histone acetylation and/or DNA-methylation, restricts the ability of ectopic transcription factors to interfere with class-specific programs in Ring1 mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work in C. elegans.

claim: Additional regulatory constraints, such as histone acetylation and/or DNA-methylation, restrict the ability of ectopic transcription factors to interfere with class-specific programs in Ring1 mutants.
source: In C. elegans the ability of transcription factors to reprogram neuronal class identity requires removal of histone deacetylase proteins (Tursun et al., 2011), suggesting that additional regulatory constraints, such as histone acetylation and/or DNA-methylation, restricts the ability of ectopic transcription factors to interfere with class-specific programs in Ring1 mutants.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the C. elegans data and the observation that MN class features are preserved in Ring1 mutants.

claim: The loss of subtype-specific programs in brachial and thoracic segments can be attributed to the attenuation of expression of rostral HoxA and HoxC cluster paralogs.
source: The loss of subtype-specific programs in brachial and thoracic segments can be attributed to the attenuation of expression of rostral HoxA and HoxC cluster paralogs, as mice lacking these Hox genes show a similar loss in MN subtype features (Jung et al., 2010; Jung et al., 2014; Philippidou et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison to previous studies on Hox mutants.

claim: Selective loss of Hox function in MNs accounts for the observation that the majority of downregulated genes in Ring1 mutants are segment-specific.
source: Selective loss of Hox function in MNs also appears to account for the observation that the majority of downregulated genes in Ring1 mutants are segment-specific.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the RNAseq data showing segment-specific downregulation of genes.

claim: In Ring1 mutants, brachial MNs ectopically express Hox9-Hox13 paralogs, while expression of Hox genes normally expressed by brachial MNs is diminished.
source: Our results indicate that in Ring1 mutants brachial MNs ectopically express Hox9-Hox13 paralogs, while expression of Hox genes normally expressed by brachial MNs is diminished.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq and immunohistochemistry data from Ring1 mutants.

claim: MNs in Ring1 mutants fail to acquire a limb-innervating LMC molecular fate, and express markers indicative of MMC and HMC subtypes.
source: As a consequence, MNs fail to acquire a limb-innervating LMC molecular fate, and express markers indicative of MMC and HMC subtypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data showing loss of LMC markers and retention of MMC/HMC markers.

claim: The Hox code of MNs is scrambled in Ring1 mutants, reverting to the fate of ancestral axial subtypes.
source: These observations are consistent with a model in which the Hox code of MNs is scrambled in Ring1 mutants, reverting to the fate of ancestral axial subtypes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective data on Hox expression and MN subtype markers in Ring1 mutants.

claim: Acute depletion of Pcgf4 (Bmi1) in chick leads to ectopic Hoxc9 expression in brachial segments and a switch of LMC neurons to a thoracic PGC fate.
source: We previously found that acute depletion of the canonical PRC1 component Pcgf4 (Bmi1) in chick leads to ectopic Hoxc9 expression in brachial segments and a switch of LMC neurons to a thoracic PGC fate (Golden and Dasen, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work from the authors' lab.

claim: In Ring1 mutants, multiple caudal Hox genes (Hox9-Hox13 paralogs) are derepressed, and the remaining MNs have an axial subtype fate.
source: By contrast in Ring1 mutants, multiple caudal Hox genes (Hox9-Hox13 paralogs) are derepressed, and the remaining MNs have an axial subtype fate.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq and immunohistochemistry data from Ring1 mutants.

claim: PRC1 is required to restrict expression of multiple cell-fate determinants throughout the rostrocaudal axis.
source: These observations indicate that PRC1 is required to restrict expression of multiple cell-fate determinants throughout the rostrocaudal axis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the RNAseq and ATACseq data showing common upregulated genes across segments.

claim: The downregulation of segment-specific genes can be attributed to the loss of Hox-dependent MN columnar subtypes, due to altered Hox gene expression in PRC1 mutants.
source: By contrast, the downregulation of segment-specific genes can be attributed to the loss of Hox-dependent MN columnar subtypes, due to altered Hox gene expression in PRC1 mutants.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the RNAseq data showing segment-specific downregulation.

claim: Removal of PRC1 leads to the derepression and increased accessibility of caudal Hox genes.
source: We found that removal of PRC1 leads to the derepression and increased accessibility of caudal Hox genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq and ATACseq data from Ring1 mutants.

claim: Loss of PRC1 does not result in a sustained derepression of all Hox genes.
source: Loss of PRC1 does not result in a sustained derepression of all Hox genes, as Hox genes normally expressed by brachial- and thoracic-level MNs are attenuated in the absence of Ring1.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq data showing selective derepression of caudal Hox genes and loss of rostral Hox expression.

claim: Loss of PRC function in Drosophila leads to ectopic expression of the caudal Hox gene Abd-b and repression of Ubx expression.
source: These findings are reminiscent of the function of PRCs in Drosophila, where loss of PRC function leads to ectopic expression of the caudal Hox gene Abd-b and repression of Ubx expression (Struhl and Akam, 1985; Struhl and White, 1985), likely reflecting cross-repressive interactions between caudal Hox proteins and rostral Hox genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies in Drosophila.

claim: Cross-repressive interactions between caudal Hox proteins and rostral Hox genes occur in Drosophila.
source: These findings are reminiscent of the function of PRCs in Drosophila, where loss of PRC function leads to ectopic expression of the caudal Hox gene Abd-b and repression of Ubx expression (Struhl and Akam, 1985; Struhl and White, 1985), likely reflecting cross-repressive interactions between caudal Hox proteins and rostral Hox genes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the cited Drosophila studies.

claim: Reduced rostral Hox gene expression in Ring1 mutants is not a reflection of reduced chromatin accessibility at these targets.
source: Notably, reduced rostral Hox gene expression in Ring1 mutants is not a reflection of reduced chromatin accessibility at these targets, consistent with a model in which this form of repression is not associated with global changes in chromatin structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by ATACseq data showing no loss of accessibility at rostral Hox genes.

claim: Derepression of Hox13 paralogs alone does not appear to account for all of the specification defects in Ring1 mutants.
source: Derepression of Hox13 paralogs alone does not appear to account for all of the specification defects in Ring1 mutants, as Hox10 paralogs (Hoxa10, Hoxc10, and Hoxd10) were expressed normally in lumbar segments.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the RNAseq data showing normal Hox10 expression in lumbar segments despite specification defects.

claim: Hoxc9 can repress Hox4-Hox8 paralogs in MNs through direct binding.
source: Hoxc9 can also repress Hox4-Hox8 paralogs in MNs through direct binding (Jung et al., 2010), and likely contributes to the Ring1 mutant phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on Hoxc9 function.

claim: Derepression of multiple caudal Hox paralogs has a cumulative effect on repressing brachial and thoracic Hox genes.
source: Derepression of multiple caudal Hox paralogs therefore appears to have a cumulative effect on repressing brachial and thoracic Hox genes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective data on Hox expression in Ring1 mutants.

claim: PRCs establish rostral Hox boundaries, while Hox cross-repressive interactions define caudal boundaries.
source: In conjunction with studies in Drosophila, these finding indicate a conserved mechanism of rostrocaudal patterning, in which PRCs establish rostral Hox boundaries, while Hox cross-repressive interactions define caudal boundaries.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective data and comparison to Drosophila studies.

claim: PRC2 activity is required to restrict gene expression in early development.
source: Studies of neuronal and non-neuronal development provide compelling evidence that PRC2 activity is required to restrict gene expression in early development (Ezhkova et al., 2009; Gentile et al., 2019; Snitow et al., 2015; Yaghmaeian Salmani et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on PRC2 function in development.

claim: Hox boundaries are unaffected after genetic removal of PRC2 function.
source: Our studies show that Hox boundaries are unaffected after genetic removal of PRC2 function, which leads to diminished H3K27me3 by the time of MN differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data from EzhMNΔ and EedNEΔ mice.

claim: Mutation of Ezh genes or Eed depletes H3K27me3 from progenitors and postmitotic neurons by E11.5, without appreciably affecting MN generation, Hox expression, or downstream Hox effectors.
source: Mutation of Ezh genes or Eed depletes H3K27me3 from progenitors and postmitotic neurons by E11.5, without appreciably affecting MN generation, Hox expression, or downstream Hox effectors.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data from EzhMNΔ and EedNEΔ mice.

claim: The axial identity of progenitor cells appears to be shaped prior to neurogenesis.
source: As the axial identity of progenitor cells appears to be shaped prior to neurogenesis (Metzis et al., 2018), our PRC2 manipulations likely remove H3K27me3 after Polycomb repression has been initiated.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on progenitor specification.

claim: PRC2 manipulations likely remove H3K27me3 after Polycomb repression has been initiated.
source: As the axial identity of progenitor cells appears to be shaped prior to neurogenesis (Metzis et al., 2018), our PRC2 manipulations likely remove H3K27me3 after Polycomb repression has been initiated.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the timing of Cre-mediated deletion and the observation that some H3K27me3 remains at E10.5.

claim: Detectable levels of H3K27me3 remain in the MN domain up until E10.5 in Ezh mutants.
source: Consistent with this idea, our analyses of Ezh mutants as well as previous analyses of EedNEΔ mice (Yaghmaeian Salmani et al., 2018), showed detectable levels of H3K27me3 in the MN domain up until E10.5, indicating that some H3K27me3 remains during the phase in which anterior Hox boundaries are established.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data from Ezh mutants and citation to previous work.

claim: Residual H3K27me3 is transmitted through cell division in PRC2 mutants and is sufficient to recruit canonical PRC1 and maintain target gene repression.
source: One plausible scenario is that residual H3K27me3 is transmitted through cell division in PRC2 mutants and is sufficient to recruit canonical PRC1 and maintain target gene repression.
evidence: This claim is speculative, representing a proposed mechanism to explain the lack of phenotypes in PRC2 mutants.

claim: During neural differentiation, the rate of cell division decreases.
source: During neural differentiation, the rate of cell division decreases (Kicheva et al., 2014; Wilcock et al., 2007), potentially limiting H3K27me3 depletion, and enabling PRC1 to bind at target loci, even in the absence of de novo H3K27 methylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on cell division during neural differentiation.

claim: Approximately 40% of residual H3K27me3 can maintain PRC repression in intestinal stem cells.
source: Consistent with this idea, recent studies on the effects of PRC2 depletion in intestinal stem cells indicate that ~40% of residual H3K27me3 can maintain PRC repression (Jadhav et al., 2020), although the extent of derepression varies with gene target.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study on PRC2 function in intestinal stem cells.

claim: Later-born oligodendrocytes derived from the MN progenitor domain depend on PRC2 function for their differentiation.
